title: The Shepherd of Hermas
hook: visions of the church as an old woman growing young, from a man once sold in Rome
tomorrow: asked to judge a brother, a desert monk brings a leaking basket. why?

segments.voice: Same streets, same food, a different home: the Letter to Diognetus. Citizens of heaven. Now a book of visions, with a strange picture of the Church.

Aging filters show a face at eighty in a few seconds: the lines, the gray. Run one backward and the years fall away. An early Christian book of visions runs it backward on purpose. It opens with a confession: its writer, Hermas, says the man who raised him sold him to a woman named Rhoda, in Rome. Then the visions begin. An elderly woman in shining clothes sits on a great chair and reads to him from a book. Hermas guesses she must be someone from the old stories. He's wrong.
screen: `AN AGING FILTER, RUN BACKWARD.` → `HERMAS, ONCE SOLD.` → `AN OLD WOMAN WITH A BOOK.`

segments.voice: A young man tells him: she is the Church. Why old? Because she was created before all things. Then the strange part. Hermas sees her three times, and each time she's younger: first old and seated, then with a younger face, standing, and at last young and full of joy. Why? She looked old, he's told, because his own spirit was old, worn down by worry and doubt. She grew younger as his spirit was renewed, the way good news lifts someone out of grief. So her age is read in the faces of the people who see her. A psalm has the same hope: "thy youth is renewed like the eagle's." Sikhs have a cousin of this. Their congregational prayer, the Ardas, closes by asking that through God's Name their spirits stay in chardi kala, rising spirits, and that by God's will all may fare well. What's shared: a people's spirit isn't fixed by its age or its troubles; it can rise again, and it's prayed for together. The honest difference: in Hermas, the one who grows young is the Church, shown in a vision, as one man's hope returns. In the Ardas, chardi kala is asked through the Name, a Sikh ideal of rising spirits even in hardship, joined to the good of everyone.
screen: `SHE IS THE CHURCH.` · `THREE VISITS, YOUNGER EACH TIME.` · `HIS SPIRIT WAS THE OLD ONE.` · `CHARDI KALA: RISING SPIRITS.` · then, large: `THE CHURCH GROWS YOUNG.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and bring to mind a community you belong to: a church, a family, a team, a circle of friends. See it first on a worn-out day, then let it grow younger in your mind as hope comes back to one person in it, then another, and stay with that picture.
The Shepherd of Hermas. An early Christian book of visions, where the Church appears as a woman who grows young.
Here's the line: the church grows young, and in the vision it happens when hope comes back. Until next time.

howItsDone: The Shepherd of Hermas isn't read in Sunday worship today, but Christians study it as one of the early writings after the New Testament, and its pictures turn up in sermons on renewal.

fork.setup: your grandfather's men's group at church is down to five, all retired. he says it 'feels old.' what does Hermas's vision suggest about a group that feels old?
options: its age shows in its spirit; hope can make it young again.
it's finished; an old group can't come back.
only new young members can make it young.
fork.reveal: in Hermas, the Church looked old because the one seeing her was worn down, and grew young as his hope returned. her age wasn't counted in years.

chat.says: our church is mostly gray hair. pop says it'll 'grow young' even after i leave. just a nice saying?
options: In Hermas, the church looks old to a worn-out spirit and grows young as hope comes back.
Yes, just a saying. Churches only grow young when teenagers join and the old members leave.
He means the church never changes. Old or young, it always looks exactly the same to everyone.
chat.meaning: In Hermas's vision the Church looked old because his spirit was worn down, and younger as hope returned. Her age is read in the faces of those who see her.

notes: Written 2026-10-13 in the year-2-4 recipe; rewritten 2026-10-15 in recipe v3 (wisdom shape: why would something old grow young?). Title, word, carry and sources kept; Psalm 103:5 and the Sikh Ardas added for the unity thread.

Unity thread (owner, 'more alike than we think'): the closing lines of the Sikh Ardas, 'Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhane sarbat da bhala', paraphrased (no translation quoted): through the Name, may spirits be ever rising (chardi kala); by your will, may all fare well. Shared: a community's spirit is not fixed by age or hardship and can rise again, prayed for together. Honest difference: in Hermas the Church is renewed in a vision as one man's hope returns; in the Ardas chardi kala is asked through the Name (Naam), a Sikh ideal kept even in hardship, joined to the good of all (sarbat da bhala). Neither ranked. Confirm with a Christian Keeper and, ideally, a Sikh reader; confirm 'congregational prayer' and the pronunciations.
The index hook calls Hermas 'a freed slave'; the lesson says only what Vision 1.1 says (he was sold to Rhoda in Rome). The teaser hook was rewritten to match.

All of Hermas is paraphrased. Confirm: Hermas's guess that the woman is the Sibyl (Vision 2.4) is rendered as 'someone from the old stories'; the three appearances and their explanation (Vision 3.10–13) are compressed; 'for her sake the world was framed' was cut for length.
The index hook names a church 'growing young'; Pop's line in the chat follows it.
Original: ποιμήν (shepherd); confirm accent and pronunciation.
Grace storyline, day 13: Grace notices her church is 'mostly gray hair'; Pop says it will 'grow young' even after she leaves. Practice kind: eyes-closed stillness.
